title: Cleft Palate
subject: Surgery
summary: Cleft palate is a congenital midline defect of the secondary palate that impairs feeding, speech and middle‑ear function. Management requires multidisciplinary repair, infection control and long‑term follow‑up, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: A cleft palate is a failure of fusion of the palatal shelves during weeks 7‑12 of gestation, producing an opening in the hard and/or soft palate.
b: Diagnosed at birth by visual inspection of the oral cavity
May be confirmed with a flexible nasendoscope if the defect is subtle

sections.p: Severity is graded by the extent of the defect and involvement of the hard versus soft palate.
b: Veau classification: I – soft palate only; II – hard palate up to incisive foramen; III – hard palate to incisive foramen + soft palate; IV – complete bilateral cleft of hard and soft palate

sections.p: Most cases are multifactorial; genetic variants and environmental exposures interact.
b: Maternal folate deficiency
Family history of cleft palate; mutations in FOXE1, IRF6, TBX22
Maternal infections common in the tropics (rubella, syphilis, malaria) and teratogenic drugs (phenytoin, retinoids)
Maternal smoking, alcohol, and poorly controlled diabetes

sections.p: Newborns with a cleft palate have characteristic feeding difficulties and may develop recurrent otitis media.
b: Nasogastric or spoon‑feeding required; milk regurgitates through the nose
Hypernasal speech after the first months of life
Middle‑ear effusion causing conductive hearing loss

t.b: Confirms location and size of the cleft; guides surgical planning
Assesses the soft palate and nasopharyngeal airway when the defect is not obvious

t.a: Audiometry (behavioural or OAE) if age >3 months
t.b: Detects conductive hearing loss from middle‑ear effusion; if unavailable, use tympanometry with a portable device

t.a: Genetic counseling / karyotype if other anomalies present
t.b: Identifies syndromic causes (e.g., 22q11.2 deletion) that affect management

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening in the newborn period and later affect growth and development.
b: Severe feeding failure leading to dehydration or malnutrition
Aspiration pneumonia from nasal regurgitation
Recurrent otitis media with hearing loss affecting language acquisition
Associated airway anomalies (e.g., tracheoesophageal fistula) that require urgent surgery

sections.p: Treatment is staged: initial feeding support, surgical repair, and long‑term multidisciplinary care.
b: Feeding: use specially designed bottles or spoon‑feeding; consider nasogastric tube if severe
Surgical repair: primary palatoplasty at 9‑12 months (or earlier if severe feeding problems); technique chosen by local expertise (e.g., von Langenbeck, Furlow)
Antibiotics: peri‑operative ampicillin‑sulbactam to prevent wound infection; avoid clindamycin in areas with high C. difficile prevalence
Ear care: insert grommets (ventilation tubes) after 6 months if chronic effusion persists; monitor hearing
Speech therapy: start after palate closure to address hypernasality

sections.p: Long‑term follow‑up focuses on growth, speech, hearing and psychosocial support.
b: Regular audiology review every 6 months until school age
Speech assessment at 2 years and yearly thereafter
Nutritional monitoring and growth charts
Counselling on folic acid supplementation for future pregnancies

sections.p: Conditions that may mimic a cleft palate or coexist.
b: Submucous cleft palate – intact mucosa with underlying muscular defect; presents with bifid uvula and hypernasal speech
Hard palate fistula after trauma or surgery – localized opening rather than congenital defect
Normal otoscopy does not rule out middle‑ear effusion; tympanometry is more reliable
A small mucosal defect may be missed on visual exam; nasendoscopy is needed

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent feeding failure despite assisted feeding
Signs of aspiration (coughing, wheeze, desaturation) after feeds
Recurrent otitis media with no improvement after antibiotics

faq.q: Why is isolated cleft palate more common in females?
faq.a: The sex difference is thought to reflect X‑linked genetic factors and hormonal influences during palate formation.

faq.q: Can a child with cleft palate have a normal speech?
faq.a: Speech can be near normal after timely repair and speech therapy, but hypernasality may persist without adequate follow‑up.

faq.q: What if I cannot obtain a nasendoscope?
faq.a: Rely on careful oral inspection and, if needed, refer for imaging (e.g., CT) or arrange a tele‑consult with a centre that has the equipment.

exam: What are the key steps in feeding a newborn with an isolated cleft palate? — Use a specialized bottle or spoon, keep the infant upright, consider nasogastric feeding if regurgitation is severe; monitor weight daily.

How does the Veau classification influence timing of surgery? — Larger (Veau III/IV) defects often need earlier repair (9‑10 months) to improve speech, while small (Veau I) defects may be delayed until 12‑14 months.

A 6‑month‑old presents with chronic otitis media and a known cleft palate. What is the next appropriate intervention? — Arrange audiometry and consider insertion of ventilation tubes to prevent hearing loss.
Which genetic mutation is specifically associated with isolated cleft palate and congenital hypothyroidism? — FOXE1 mutation; it explains the thyroid phenotype and hair changes.

In a low‑resource hospital without grommets, how would you manage persistent middle‑ear effusion? — Perform regular ear cleaning, use topical antibiotics if infected, and refer for hearing assessment; prioritize speech therapy.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a newborn with cleft palate? — Signs of aspiration pneumonia (tachypnea, desaturation) or severe dehydration despite feeding attempts.

Why is ampicillin‑sulbactam preferred for peri‑operative prophylaxis in this setting? — Broad coverage against oral flora and low resistance rates; clindamycin is avoided due to high C. difficile risk.
How would you differentiate a submucous cleft palate from an overt cleft palate on exam? — Look for a bifid uvula, zona pellucida, and a palpable muscular gap; the mucosa remains intact.
